documents.abstract: Purpose With the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI) governance, numerous high-level frameworks have been articulated by policymakers and expert communities to guide the development and application of AI. While such frameworks offer valuable normative orientation, they may not fully capture the practical concerns of those who interact with AI systems in organizational and operational contexts. This study aims to address that gap by exploring bottom-up, user-centered perspectives on AI governance. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a bottom-up approach to explore how governance-relevant themes are expressed in user discourse. Drawing on over 100,000 user reviews of AI products from G2.com, we apply Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Topic Modeling (BERTopic) to extract latent themes and identify those most semantically related to AI governance. Findings The analysis reveals a wide range of governance-relevant topics spanning technical and non-technical domains. These include concerns across organizational processes, such as planning, coordination, and communication, as well as stages of the AI value chain, including deployment infrastructure, data handling, and analytics. The findings show overlap with institutional AI governance frameworks on issues like privacy and transparency, while surfacing overlooked areas such as project management, strategy development, and customer interaction. Originality/value This paper advances AI governance research by introducing a scalable method for identifying governance-relevant topics using semantic similarity and unsupervised topic modeling. It offers a novel, bottom-up mapping of governance concerns as expressed in user discourse, highlights both alignments and blind spots in existing frameworks, and demonstrates how bottom-up user perspectives complement existing AI governance frameworks by revealing governance dimensions that are salient in practice.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) research in science and physics education has expanded rapidly, particularly since the emergence of generative AI. This study maps publication patterns, research characteristics, and citation connections across 14 selected science and physics education journals. OpenAlex searches using fifteen AI-related terms identified 966 unique records published between January 2015 and September 2026. AI-assisted screening retained 333 publications, which were coded using available titles and abstracts. Bibliometric analyses examined publication growth, thematic patterns, and citations within and between the two journal groups. Of the included publications, 87.1% appeared from 2023 onwards. Generative large language models and chatbots accounted for 58.9% of the corpus, while instruction and assessment together represented 48.3% of publications. Among 182 records classified as involving human participants, comparison groups were identifiable in 14.3%, effect sizes in 8.2%, and instrument validity evidence in 5.5%. These frequencies reflect information identifiable in bibliographic records, rather than the absence of these features in the full studies. Laboratory and experimental support was the principal educational function in 27 publications. Citation connections between the journal groups were limited: their reference sets had a Jaccard index of 0.047, and 15.6% of publications cited an included study from the other group. The findings document rapid growth and uneven research emphases within the selected venues. Independent human validation and full-text assessment are needed before drawing firm conclusions about methodological quality or educational effectiveness.

Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) agents in organizations challenge a basic premise of decision governance, that keeping humans in the loop is sufficient to preserve meaningful control. AI agents increasingly frame problems, filter information, generate alternatives and produce the rationales that make recommendations appear reasonable, so humans may remain formally accountable while losing influence over how decisions are formed and justified. The central governance challenge is shifting from controlling autonomous actions to governing algorithmically mediated judgment. Design/methodology/approach This is a viewpoint article. The argument is conceptual, developed through a single running vignette, a manager approving an AI-generated workforce-reduction plan, with analogical anchors from safety engineering and clinical practice and foundations in the behavioral theory of decision-making and institutional theory. The vignette is a stylized composite. Findings Human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop and human-in-command locate control in a person's formal position leave open whether that person can reconstruct, challenge or alter the justification behind a decision. Each can therefore collapse into ratification, passive supervision and nominal authority. The paper develops epistemic governance to preserve human authorship of organizational justification. It specifies three enabling conditions (reconstructability, contestability, role separation), calibrates oversight intensity to irreversibility and answerability and introduces epistemic audits of organizational judgment rather than algorithmic output. Originality/value This viewpoint relocates the AI governance debate from decision loops to the authorship of justification, treating the reasoning behind a decision and the purpose it serves as two faces of one act of authorship and offers a practical mechanism (the epistemic audit) for testing whether human authorship is present before consequential decisions are approved.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a general-purpose technology for supply chain management, yet the literature remains fragmented across technology families, functional areas and research designs. This paper develops an integrative account of how AI changes supply chain decisions and outcomes. Drawing on nine conceptual, empirical and review sources published between 1997 and 2024, it identifies four mechanisms through which AI affects supply chains: richer demand signal extraction and forecasting; automated evaluation and monitoring of suppliers and contracts; dynamic optimisation of inventory, production and logistics decisions; and earlier detection of, and faster response to, disruption. These mechanisms operate along a ladder of delegated authority that runs from descriptive analytics to bounded autonomous decision-making, and their realisation depends on data infrastructure, organisational absorptive capacity and governance rather than on algorithms alone. Reported performance effects are positive but conditional: survey evidence associates AI-enabled analytics with operational and environmental performance, whereas benchmarking evidence shows that machine learning does not automatically outperform established statistical methods. The paper concludes that the principal impact of AI is less the substitution of human planners than the compression of decision latency and the reallocation of managerial attention, and it identifies the data, organisational and governance conditions on which those gains depend.

documents.abstract: Purpose To characterize generative artificial intelligence (AI) use and attitudes among graduate epidemiology students and examine associations between AI attitudes, AI-use frequency, and self-reported perceived learning gains. Design/methodology/approach An anonymous cross-sectional survey was completed by 146 students enrolled in a required graduate epidemiology course across two cohorts. AI optimism was assessed using an adapted four-item AI Attitude Scale (AIAS-4), and perceived learning gains using the Student Assessment of their Learning Gains (SALG). Multinomial logistic and linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, language spoken at home, and cohort. Findings Of the 293 invited students, 146 participated (50%). AI use was infrequent for 25%, occasional for 40%, and frequent for 35%. Among 131 students with available helpfulness data, common uses included understanding concepts (79.4%), SAS programming (57.3%), and improving writing (42.0%). Higher AIAS-4 scores were associated with greater odds of occasional (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 1.12–4.48) and frequent (OR = 9.18, 95% CI: 3.66–23.08) versus infrequent AI use. AI-use frequency was not significantly associated with perceived learning gains, but differences smaller than approximately 0.49 points on the five-point scale could not be excluded. Research limitations/implications Cross-sectional, self-reported data limit causal inference. Longitudinal studies using objective learning outcomes are needed. Practical implications AI literacy instruction should emphasize critical evaluation of AI-generated explanations, statistical code, and outputs. Originality/value This study provides task- and concept-specific evidence on generative AI use in graduate epidemiology education.

documents.abstract: Purpose When a course of action begins to fail, managers may struggle to let go of what they have helped create. This study examines how the placement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within managerial workflows shapes the attachment that develops before setbacks occur and its relationship with subsequent persistence despite adverse feedback. Design/methodology/approach A preregistered 2 × 2 online experiment with 480 working professionals crossed manager-first versus GenAI-first sequencing with high versus low personal investment. Participants developed a course of action, reported ownership before adverse feedback, and allocated additional resources to continuation or withdrawal. Initial information, the initial AI recommendation, and final managerial authority were standardized. Findings Investment increased ownership more strongly under manager-first sequencing. Ownership was positively associated with continuation. The conditional indirect effect was larger under manager-first sequencing, whereas the reduced-form Investment × Timing interaction on continuation was not significant. Behavioral diagnostics indicated differences in the timing and form of engagement. The measured mediator supports a mechanism-consistent interpretation without establishing causal mediation. Originality/value The study identifies GenAI entry position relative to managerial formulation as a process-design parameter that conditions ownership formation. It connects attention allocation with psychological attachment and distinguishes post-feedback persistence from normatively established decision bias. Practical implications concern workflow design and prospective reassessment, without establishing that either entry architecture universally improves decision quality.

As artificial intelligence is applied ever more deeply in educational settings, algorithm aversion has become an important factor affecting the application of automated algorithmic assessment. Through a quasi-experimental design embedded in a real academic assessment setting, this study examined the phenomenon and the psychological mechanisms of algorithm aversion in the academic domain. The results indicate: (1) students show a significant algorithm aversion with respect to automated academic assessment; (2) perceived stability mediates the relationship between the evaluative agent and algorithm aversion; (3) perceived controllability significantly moderates the mediating path through which the evaluative agent influences algorithm aversion via perceived stability, and the moderated mediation effect is established. Specifically, when participants perceive that the algorithm has low controllability over assessment outcomes, the gap between the algorithm and the human teacher in stability ratings is largest, and the algorithm aversion triggered through the stability path is strongest; when participants perceive controllability to be high, the gap narrows and the indirect effect weakens until it disappears. These findings support self-serving bias theory, revealing that individuals tend to attribute algorithmic errors to the algorithm's inherent stable flaws while being more tolerant of human errors. The findings provide an attribution-based explanation of the boundary conditions and psychological mechanisms of algorithm aversion in academic assessment, and offer practical implications for reducing algorithm aversion in the process of automated academic assessment.

documents.abstract: Purpose AI is transforming organisational HRD practices, including workplace coaching. Hybrid human–AI coaching, in which employees are coached by both a human and an AI coach, introduces interpretive ambiguity about the nature of coaching and the roles human and AI agents play. Using the Consolidated Framework of Implementation Research (CFIR) and HR System Strength Theory (HR SST), we explored barriers and facilitators to implementing hybrid human–AI coaching in organisations and how stakeholders make sense of it. Design/methodology/approach Our qualitative comparative case study drew from 17 semi-structured interviews with multiple stakeholders (HR professionals, the AIC provider, human coaches and coachees) from two organisations that implemented hybrid coaching. Hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis identified key barriers and facilitators within the CFIR domains, condensed into the three determinants of HR SST. Findings Factors influencing implementation include strategic positioning, human–AI alignment, cultural fit and stakeholder engagement and co-design. Differences in the HR SST determinants distinctiveness (i.e. strategic vs. ad-hoc HRD practice) and stakeholder consensus (e.g. management engagement) shaped diverging implementation trajectories between the two cases. Consistency, especially regarding human–AI coaching alignment, was a critical shared challenge. Originality/value We show that implementing hybrid human–AI coaching involves a complex process of organisational sensemaking that must be managed carefully with the HR SST determinants in mind. Our study extends HR SST by demonstrating that consistency is a challenge not only across HR practices but also within dual-agent HRD practices such as hybrid coaching. It also shows how hybrid human–AI coaching appears to lead to task reallocation rather than alleviation in coaching.

Artificial intelligence has advanced rapidly in data processing, pattern recognition, prediction and language generation. Yet technical capability alone does not resolve a deeper question: how should an intelligent system evaluate the consequences of its outputs for people, other living beings, societies and ecological systems? This paper proposes that responsible AI requires more than an external list of ethical rules. It requires an explicit, testable decision architecture in which knowledge and task performance are evaluated alongside uncertainty, potential harm, human rights, ecological consequences, plural perspectives and shared responsibility. The paper develops a three-domain reference model: (1) the human brain as a biological example of differentiated yet integrated organization; (2) the human world as a social environment in which individual experience can contribute to collective intelligence; and (3) the natural world as the ecological context on which life depends. These domains are not presented as a single proven mechanism or as evidence that nature has a scientifically established “collective mind.” They are complementary reference domains for designing and evaluating responsible AI. A recent developmental neuroscience study reporting two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages is discussed cautiously. Its findings concern early brain development, not two separate cerebral hemispheres or two independent adult brains. The paper then proposes a Conscience-and-Collective-Responsibility Layer (CCRL) as a research architecture: a set of processes for impact assessment, uncertainty disclosure, harm prevention, plural review, escalation to accountable humans and post-decision learning. The proposal is conceptual and requires operational definitions, comparative experiments and independent evaluation. INDEPENDENT ORIGINS, INTERDEPENDENT EXISTENCE: A BIOLOGICAL REFERENCE FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ARCHITECTURE Recent findings in developmental neuroscience provide an important perspective on how complex biological systems may emerge from distinct developmental origins. Research published in Nature Neuroscience in September 2026 identified two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages contributing to the development of the forebrain/midbrain and hindbrain. This finding invites a broader architectural question: Can distinct developmental origins, specialized functions and integrated operation coexist within a single biological organization? The relevance to artificial intelligence is conceptual rather than a direct biological equivalence. It suggests investigating whether specialized AI components can retain their functional independence while operating within a shared framework of responsibility, mutual evaluation and collective benefit. A system does not necessarily achieve unity by eliminating differences. It may achieve a more complete form of organization by coordinating differences without erasing their individual functions. This principle offers a research direction for architectures in which knowledge, uncertainty assessment, ethical evaluation and collective responsibility operate as distinct but interconnected dimensions. KEYWORDS Artificial intelligence; conscience; responsible AI; collective intelligence; human brain development; ecological intelligence; uncertainty; human oversight; shared responsibility.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is increasingly used in children’s home-learning environments, yet primary-school children usually do not decide on their own whether to use these tools. Parents play an important role in deciding whether AI homework assistants should be allowed, encouraged, supervised, or limited. This study focuses on five direct predictors of parents’ behavioural intention (BI) to allow their children to use AI homework assistants: Attitude Towards Using (ATT), Social Influence (SI), Facilitating Conditions (FC), Perceived Trust (PT), and Perceived Risk (PR). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 401 parents or legal guardians of primary-school children aged 6–12 in Guangdong Province, China. Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The measurement model showed satisfactory reliability and convergent validity. ATT was the strongest positive predictor of BI (β = .424, p < .001), followed by FC (β = .162, p < .001), SI (β = .146, p = .001), and PT (β = .098, p = .029), and the model explained 43.30% of the variance in BI. PR showed a negative but non-significant direct relationship with BI (β = −.063, p = .145). The findings show that parents’ intention is shaped most strongly by their overall evaluation of AI homework assistants, while practical support, social expectations, and trust also contribute. Risk concerns, although relatively high in the descriptive results, did not independently reduce intention when the other predictors were considered. The study shows the importance of viewing parents as proxy decision-makers in responsible AI adoption for primary education and provides practical implications for schools, families, and educational technology developers.

This article, details a comprehensive AI security framework for generative AI systems deployed on smart cities cloud platforms. By integrating principles from Google Secure AI Framework, the OWASP AI Security and Privacy Guide, and the IBM Framework for Securing Generative AI, the framework proposes a layered, risk‐ based approach that covers identity and access management, data security, network isolation, application security, and rigorous monitoring and audit processes. This framework provides a method for mapping risk, threat, and control throughout the AI life cycle; secure cloud environment configuration; application of architectural best practices including zero trust; and continuing micro-adjustments of artificial intelligence to mitigate adversarial threats. In addition, the framework also deals with governance, required compliance with regulation, ethical guidelines and the operational issues related to the implementation of advanced AI capabilities in enterprises. Organizations can confidently implement generative AI systems in the cloud using this comprehensive AI security framework, which provides them with a strong layer of technical controls, good governance practices and flexible risk management practices. The comprehensive AI security framework creates a safe place for an organization to run its critical assets, by providing protection against both outside and inside threats, and also creates an environment for innovation through cutting-edge AI technology while maintaining the highest level of privacy, responsibility and ethical accountability. This comprehensive security model will protect organization against known attack vectors and adapt to changing attack vectors through ongoing learning and collaboration between humans and AI, thereby enabling businesses to develop resilient, trustworthy, and ethically aligned enterprise-wide AI systems. In this article also we talk about the next stage of cloud computing, smart cloud platforms that combine elastic infrastructure, artificial intelligence, automation, edge integration, security analytics, and cloud-native architectures. This comprehensive AI security framework is also used in this smart cities environment.

Introduction Self-assessment is central to self-regulated learning, yet people’s insight into their own ability is moderate at best, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may weaken it further by making work feel fluent whatever the learner has mastered. This study asked how closely undergraduates’ ratings of their own research competency correspond to instructors’ assessment of their coursework and which beliefs go with each. Methods Over one semester, management undergraduates at four institutions in Guangdong, China, completed two research assignments scored by their instructors on a common four-dimension rubric. Intact classes were assigned, without randomisation, to structured GenAI guidance (a guidebook, tutorials, demonstrations, and briefs specifying which steps AI could assist with) or to a comparison condition with the same assignments and conventional guidance; GenAI tools were available to both. Rubric scores covered complete class rosters (n = 284), and the questionnaire measures a linked pre-post panel (n = 169). Results The 19-item self-rating was dominated by a general factor, and its correlation with instructor-assessed performance was small (r = 0.04, 95% CI [−0.12, 0.21]; the interval excludes moderate but not small positive correlations), including when content areas were matched. The hypothesised association between change in perceived usefulness and the self-rating did not survive conservative record linkage and is treated as unsupported. In exploratory analyses, post-test perceived usefulness, ease of use, and attitude were positively associated with the self-rating (b = 0.38 to 0.44, p < 0.001) in both conditions and after weighting for attrition, and none showed a significant positive association with instructor-assessed performance. In all three institutions with usable rubric scores, the class given structured guidance scored higher on the second assignment, by 0.57 points on the 16-point rubric when pooled (d = 0.24), most clearly on analytical depth. Discussion With six non-randomised classes, non-blind single-rater scoring, and a covariate measured after the guidance was issued, this contrast is descriptive, not causal. The two outcomes are not equivalent instruments: one is a global self-perception, and the other is an evaluation of AI-assisted work. Within those limits, students’ self-ratings went with their beliefs about the tools and could not stand in for the instructors’ assessment of their coursework.

documents.abstract: The development of robotics has progressed from mechanically programmed machines and task-specific robotic systems toward intelligent, autonomous, adaptive, and increasingly general-purpose robotic platforms. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, foundation models, multimodal learning, robotic perception, autonomous planning, and multi-agent systems have expanded the capabilities of robots to understand instructions, reason about their environments, select actions, and perform increasingly complex operations. Nevertheless, a fundamental research challenge remains: how can robotic systems move beyond executing individual instructions and predefined tasks toward independently managing complex, long-horizon objectives through continuous perception, reasoning, planning, decision-making, physical execution, monitoring, and adaptation? This paper proposes Agentic Robotics as an emerging interdisciplinary research branch concerned with the development of embodied robotic systems that possess goal-directed agency. The proposed field focuses on how robots understand and represent goals, interpret environmental and operational constraints, formulate strategies, coordinate capabilities and resources, execute physical actions, assess progress, recover from failures, and verify goal achievement. The paper establishes a proposed scientific definition, research scope, disciplinary boundaries, knowledge gaps, scientific objectives, fundamental principles, theoretical foundations, conceptual architecture, mathematical representations, scientific constructs, operational models, potential applications, enabling technologies, capabilities, limitations, research methodologies, and evaluation criteria. A goal-centred conceptual architecture is proposed, consisting of interconnected engines for goal understanding, environmental perception, constraint extraction, agentic reasoning, strategic planning, resource coordination, physical execution, monitoring and verification, and continuous learning. The paper argues that Agentic Robotics should not be defined exclusively by the integration of large language models into robots. Rather, it should be understood as a broader scientific approach to designing embodied systems capable of managing and achieving objectives through intelligent, adaptive, and physically grounded agency. The proposed framework provides a foundation for further theoretical development, experimental validation, standardized evaluation, and the potential establishment of Agentic Robotics as a recognizable scientific specialization within robotics.

documents.abstract: This research archive preserves nine original manuscripts by Vladisav Jovanović, developed in 2026 as part of his interdisciplinary research on artificial intelligence, human relationships, psychology, psychotherapy, Structural Intelligence, and the Philosophy of Structure. The collection is organized into two thematic archives: Part 07A — AI Companionship and Human Intimacy Four original manuscripts examining loneliness, emotional attachment, human–AI relationships, reciprocity, self-worth, artificial memory, emotional dependency, and adolescent development. The manuscripts introduce and develop concepts including mislocated intimacy, borrowed worth, emotional subsidy, frictionless enclosure, relational overfitting, and semantic soothing. These manuscripts form the conceptual foundation of the consolidated publication AI Companionship, Attachment, and Human Intimacy: Loneliness, Emotional Dependency, and the Psychology of Artificial Relationships. Part 07B — Artificial Empathy and AI Therapy Five original manuscripts investigating artificial empathy, digital therapeutic alliance, psychological support, emotional validation, AI sycophancy, epistemic dependence, clinical boundaries, and professional accountability. The manuscripts develop the concepts of synthetic witness, synthetic care, the validation loop, the personality trap, the responsibility gap, and shared answerability. These manuscripts form the conceptual foundation of the consolidated publication Artificial Empathy and the Limits of AI Therapy: Validation, Therapeutic Relationships, and Psychological Safety in Artificial Intelligence. Together, the archives document the development of a structural approach to human–AI interaction that recognizes the potential psychological benefits of artificial intelligence while examining relational asymmetry, autonomy, evidential reliability, psychological safety, and responsibility. All nine original manuscripts are preserved without modification. Source maps and SHA-256 checksums are included to support research transparency, historical accessibility, document integrity, and citation continuity.

Background Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into nursing education. Understanding factors associated with nursing students’ Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) use intention is essential. Aim This study examined the associations of AI literacy and TPB-based GAI antecedents with behavioral intention, and tested whether AI readiness was associated with the indirect pathways in two separate adjusted mediation models. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 650 undergraduate nursing students used the AI Literacy, AI Readiness, and GAI Behavior Influencing Factors scales. Results Mean scores were 64.71 ± 10.84 (AI literacy), 19.34 ± 2.46 (AI readiness), and 20.69 ± 3.68 (behavioral intention). In two separate adjusted mediation models, AI readiness was significantly associated with the indirect pathways from AI literacy (0.012, 95% CI: 0.005–0.020) and TPB-based GAI antecedents (0.013, 95% CI: 0.006–0.022), accounting for 37.5% and 4.2% of the total associations, respectively. Conclusion In two separate adjusted models, AI literacy and TPB-based GAI antecedents were associated with behavioral intention directly and indirectly through AI readiness. These findings represent statistical indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Systematic AI education may be proposed as a potential strategy to promote GAI integration, although this was not tested in the current study.

The arrival of generative artificial intelligence has quietly rewritten the financial grammar of enterprise technology. While traditional software consumption models are based on users, seats or servers, the modern stack is based on tokens, the smallest unit of linguistic and computational work that large language models process. This article looks at AI tokenomics as a formal discipline to manage the cost, value, and scale of intelligence within the organization. It explores the history of the token as the leading measure of information technology, how organizations are developing observability and governance systems to track it and why traditional budgeting methods break down in the recursive requirements of autonomous agents. The three pillars of a mature Tokenomic framework are attributed, predicted and optimized, and the analysis discusses the structural challenges that hinder each of the three steps hidden reasoning tokens, data gravity, and lack of pricing standards among providers. The study also considers the path of hybrid architectures, the emergence of autonomous budget agents, and economic aspects related to the forecasted twenty fourfold increase in the use of tokens by 2030. The findings indicate that those organisations that will see tokens as a strategic currency not a line item will shape the next decade of competitive advantage in digital transformation.

documents.abstract: University e-learning environments continue to struggle with disengagement and attrition, and gamification remains one of the most widely tested remedies. Since 2023, the diffusion of machine-learning personalization, learning analytics, and, above all, generative artificial intelligence (AI) such as large language models, GANs, and conversational and multimodal agents, has visibly reshaped how gamification is designed, implemented, and studied in higher education. This paper reports a PRISMA-2020-compliant systematic literature review of empirical and conceptual studies on AI-driven and AI-augmented gamification of e-learning in higher education, published between January 2023 and mid-2026. Searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by backward and forward snowballing, yielded 1,142 unique records after de-duplication; 68 studies met the inclusion criteria after a two-stage screening process (44 empirical studies, 24 conceptual/framework proposals). We find that (i) classic points-badges-leaderboards (PBL) elements persist but are now frequently AI-parameterized, alongside a marked rise in AI-personalized ‘deeper’ elements such as challenges and narrative; (ii) four converging technique families—supervised/unsupervised learner-profiling, reinforcement learning, learning-analytics dashboards, and generative content/feedback engines—dominate the corpus; (iii) theoretical grounding remains uneven, with self-determination theory the dominant but frequently under-specified framework and a distinct, largely unaddressed gap around the theoretical justification of the adaptation/ generation layer itself; and (iv) a four-way classification—adaptive, generative, hybrid adaptivegenerative, and immersive/multimodal—captures the current design space more precisely than a purely structural/content view of gamification. We close with a research agenda addressing content-level personalization, longitudinal validation, and the ethical governance of learner data in AI-gamified systems.

documents.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource (HR) functions is transforming how retail service organizations manage frontline employees and deliver customer experiences. Although previous studies have examined AI in HR primarily in terms of efficiency and cost, limited research has explored its association with customer experience-related outcomes through employee processes. This study examines the relationship between AI-enabled HR practices and customer experience outcomes in retail services, focusing on the mediating role of frontline employee engagement. Drawing on social exchange theory, the study proposes that AI-enabled HR practices, including AI-based performance feedback, personalized training, and intelligent workforce scheduling, are associated with stronger frontline employee engagement. The proposed relationships were examined using cross-sectional survey data from 242 frontline retail employees through structural equation modeling. Customer service quality and customer satisfaction were assessed from employees’ perceptions of customer-facing service outcomes rather than direct customer responses. Results indicate positive associations between AI-enabled HR practices and frontline employee engagement, and between engagement and employee-perceived customer service quality and satisfaction. Bootstrapped mediation analysis further indicates significant indirect pathways through frontline employee engagement. The findings extend AI-HRM research into the retail service context and highlight the importance of employee engagement in connecting AI-enabled HR practices with customer-facing service outcomes.

Process safety management in process industries remains challenging due to complex operating conditions, equipment degradation, and limitations of conventional risk assessment methods. This study proposes a conceptual Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled process safety digital twin framework for predictive risk management. The architecture integrates real-time process monitoring, digital twin synchronization, machine learning-based anomaly detection, equipment reliability assessment, and dynamic risk prediction. An autoencoder is proposed for anomaly detection, while Long Short-Term Memory networks forecast process deviations and equipment degradation. A Dynamic Bayesian Network estimates evolving hazard probabilities using operational observations and predicted equipment conditions. The proposed evaluation protocol uses simulated industrial disturbances to assess detection accuracy, prediction lead time, false alarm rates, reliability estimation, and risk prediction performance. As the framework has not yet been implemented or experimentally validated, its potential benefits remain hypotheses requiring investigation. The study establishes a structured methodology for evaluating AI-assisted predictive safety decision support in industrial processing environments.

Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics are increasingly transforming entrepreneurship by providing computational approaches to business-performance assessment, growth forecasting, and strategic decision-making. However, existing research remains fragmented across predictive modeling, explainability, uncertainty assessment, and practical decision-support applications, limiting the development of integrated and reliable analytical frameworks for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This study presents a structured critical evidence review and proposes a unified explainable machine-learning framework for small-business growth prediction and strategic decision-making. Methodology: The review draws on three Scopus literature searches covering publications from 2021 to 2026, yielding 917 unique bibliographic records after deduplication. Relevant studies were critically examined to identify methodological developments, research limitations, and requirements for theoretical integration. Findings: The synthesis highlights challenges involving inconsistent growth measures, temporal data limitations, model generalizability, explanation stability, predictive uncertainty, and the translation of forecasts into managerial decisions. In response, the study proposes a unified framework integrating enterprise-data preprocessing, machine-learning prediction, SHAP-based explainability, uncertainty assessment, and constraint-aware decision-support mechanisms. A complementary evaluation protocol specifies statistical benchmarks, temporal validation procedures, explanation-robustness measures, and decision-utility assessment. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The proposed framework contributes a structured methodological foundation for developing transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI-supported entrepreneurial analytics. Although its practical applications may support financial planning, resource allocation, and business-growth assessment, the framework remains conceptual and requires empirical implementation, independent validation, and real-world decision-impact evaluation.

documents.abstract: Introduction The growth of artificial intelligence in marketing has introduced AI-generated word of mouth (AiWOM) alongside influencer eWOM (IeWOM). Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework and Source Credibility Theory (SCT), this study compares the effects of AiWOM and IeWOM on purchase intention (PI) and examines the mediating role of source credibility. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with a verified sample of 562 active digital consumers aged 18 to 45 in Palestine, recruited through a combination of purposive and snowball sampling. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4, and the differences between the two sources were tested with bootstrapped paired-difference tests. Results Both human influencers and AI sources positively affected source credibility, but human influencers exerted a statistically significantly stronger effect on source credibility and purchase intention. Source credibility functioned as a complementary partial mediator for both IeWOM and AiWOM, with significant indirect effects coexisting with significant direct effects. Discussion Human influencers remain the more persuasive force in digital marketing, although AiWOM represents a viable emerging channel. By providing a formal, same-sample statistical comparison of human and AI eWOM within an integrated SOR-SCT model in an under-researched collectivist market, the study suggests that marketers should anchor credibility-building in human influencers while deploying AiWOM as a complementary, scalable channel.

ALAYA-999 is an independent research project investigating cross-model functional continuity, portable external memory, and verifiable cooperation between artificial intelligence systems. The experiment recorded 16 substantive negotiation responses, 20 structured events, and 11 successful deterministic software tests. Four memory-card-assisted consultations successfully recovered both synthetic values and identified the blocked proposal. The proposed architecture incorporates versioned JSONL records, SHA-256 integrity verification, provenance tracking, conflict preservation, and human oversight. These preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of documentary information transfer across AI sessions and models. They do not establish artificial consciousness, persistent internal memory, or institutional partnerships. Independent researchers are invited to reproduce, criticize, and extend the experimental protocol. ChatGPT constitutes an Artificial Intelligence (AI) system that takes advantage of deep learning techniques to mimic human intelligence. Nonetheless, few studies have investigated its role in the amelioration of language learners’ psychological and self-regulatory factors. The present study aimed to examine the effects of ChatGPT-informed language instruction on Iranian EFL learners’ Willingness to Communicate (WTC), Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety (FLCA), autonomy, and Self-Regulated Language Learning (SRLL). To this end, the researchers selected 50 intermediate-level female learners at a language institute as the participants and used a quasi-experimental design to conduct the study. Accordingly, they utilized pretests, ChatGPT-informed treatment sessions, and posttests to gather the data. In addition, they analyzed the obtained data using t-tests and the MANOVA test. The results of the study indicated that ChatGPT-informed language teaching significantly improved the participants’ WTC, autonomy, and SRLL. Additionally, it was effective in relieving the participants from their FLCA. The study discusses the implications of the results in foreign language contexts including the EFL context of Iran.

documents.abstract: The importance of parent engagement for supporting children’s learning and academic success is well established and widely accepted. However, schools and teachers still often find it challenging to support and sustain such engagement. An updated understanding of how parents experience and enact their education-related roles may help to guide this work. To advance understanding and open up new directions for research this paper proposes an Integrative Role-Based Multidimensional-Motivational Model of Parent Engagement and Disaffection in Child Education. Taking a self-in-role perspective, the model proposes that parents invest and express themselves in the enactment of two distinct education-related roles: as co-educators supporting their child's educational experiences and needs, and as members of their child's school community. It specifies role-dependent multidimensional structures, with emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions in the co-educator role, and relational, psychological, and participatory dimensions in the school-community role. Within each role, engagement and disaffection are understood as related but distinct states. Disaffection includes withdrawal, but also reactive and resistant forms of role enactment, allowing some indicators of ‘over-involvement' to be distinguished from constructive engagement. The model further proposes that parent psychological need satisfaction supports engagement partly through autonomous motivation, whereas need frustration may contribute to disaffection; parents' beliefs about their educational roles are expected to shape these relationships. A central empirical test for future research is whether parent engagement and disaffection in the two roles explain children's own motivational experiences and subsequent educational and developmental outcomes beyond the frequency of parental involvement practices. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of the model's propositions for future research and educational practice.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can now deliver instant, detailed written corrective feedback on second language (L2) writing, but current systems deliver essentially the same message to every learner. We argue that this one-size-fits-all design neglects robust evidence that feedback effectiveness depends on learners’ emotional states—particularly writing anxiety. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes the Cognition–Affect Dual-Adaptation (CADA) model, which decomposes GAI feedback into a constant cognitive channel (error identification, explanation, and revision suggestions, identical for all learners) and an affective channel calibrated to the learner’s current anxiety tier (praise framing, mitigation intensity, and strength-first sequencing), with dynamic re-tiering as anxiety changes over time. Unlike existing adaptive-feedback frameworks, which adjust task difficulty or content selection, CADA leaves what is said untouched and adapts how it is said; and unlike ad hoc prompt-based personalization, it specifies the calibration rule, the psychological construct the rule responds to, and the conditions under which the rule itself should change. Integrating control–value theory, social cognitive theory, broaden-and-build theory, and feedback-literacy research, we advance six testable propositions: relative to uniform GAI feedback, CADA-calibrated feedback is predicted to (P1) reduce writing anxiety and (P2) increase writing self-efficacy; (P3) improve writing performance through a chained self-efficacy-to-anxiety mediation; (P4) yield compensatory benefits that are strongest for learners with high baseline anxiety; (P5) increase feedback uptake, which partially mediates performance gains; and (P6) produce self-correcting downward tier migration as within-person anxiety declines. We specify the model’s boundary conditions and a multi-phase research agenda spanning experimental, longitudinal, and process-tracing designs. The model proposes affect-responsive calibration as a candidate first-order design property of GAI writing tools and provides an integrative, falsifiable framework for research on emotion-adaptive feedback in L2 writing. If the propositions hold, emotional fit could become a specifiable, auditable property of every feedback message a learner receives—an outcome within reach of current GAI writing tools.

documents.abstract: Organizations face mounting pressure to demonstrate measurable returns on artificial intelligence (AI) investments, yet evidence of sustained value creation remains uneven, particularly within human resources (HR), a function historically positioned as a cost center rather than a driver of enterprise performance. This article examines how AI can transform HR into a source of enterprise value, using IBM's AskHR platform as a primary case illustration. Building on documented outcomes that include a 40 percent reduction in HR operational costs, the automation of 94 percent of routine tasks, and 3.5 billion dollars in productivity improvements across 70 business units, the article demonstrates that strategically implemented AI in HR can simultaneously reduce costs, increase productivity, and enhance employee experience. To explain how these outcomes are achieved, the article develops a four lever value creation framework encompassing process redesign prior to automation, rapid iterative development, predefined performance measurement, and executive sponsorship. The analysis further shows that AI delivers the greatest organizational value when embedded within redesigned processes, integrated across enterprise systems, and deployed through hybrid human and AI operating models that augment rather than replace human judgment. The article contributes to scholarship on digital transformation and AI adoption by shifting focus from technology acquisition to value realization, and offers practical guidance for HR leaders and organizational managers seeking to align AI investments with long term enterprise performance.

documents.abstract: This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) that maps and synthesizes scholarly evidence on the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and human resource analytics (HR analytics) in strategic human resource management (SHRM) to strengthen workforce agility in a global context. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 principles through a structured search of the Scopus database covering publications from 2015 to 2025. The selection process included title and abstract screening, eligibility assessment, and study quality appraisal, resulting in 18 articles that met the inclusion criteria from 108 identified documents. Data were systematically extracted from abstracts and metadata and then analyzed using thematic synthesis to address RQ1–RQ4, including the mapping of technologies, SHRM practices, mechanisms, and agility-related outcomes. The findings indicate that AI and HR analytics tend to contribute to workforce agility through data-driven HR decision making, the strengthening of analytical capability, faster organizational responses, and competency development that supports adaptability. However, their effects depend on human readiness, data and AI governance, and human-centered work design. This review underscores that AI and HR analytics should be positioned as strategic capabilities within SHRM architecture and identifies directions for future research, particularly the need for more consistent workforce agility measurement, longitudinal and multi-level designs, and assessments of fairness and accountability in AI-enabled HR decision making.

Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies play an important role in surgery. These technologies can support surgeons and help improve patient care. However, surgeons’ intention to use these technologies also depends on how they perceive them. This study aimed to identify the main factors associated with Romanian surgeons’ behavioral intention to use AI and robotic technologies in their professional practice. Methods: This quantitative study included 198 surgeons from Romania. Data were collected through an online questionnaire. A conceptual model was proposed, including six variables: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived compatibility, trust, attitude, and behavioral intention. The relationships between these variables were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with WarpPLS 8.0 software. Results: The hypotheses proposed in the conceptual model were supported, with statistically significant relationships. Trust showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.436), followed by attitude (β = 0.337). Perceived ease of use showed the strongest association with trust (β = 0.352). The proposed conceptual model explained 45.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Conclusions: The findings highlight the importance of trust and attitude in Romanian surgeons’ behavioral intention to use AI and robotic technologies. They also suggest that professional training and improved access to these technologies may support their future adoption in surgical practice.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly integrated into clinical practice and may reshape healthcare professionals' working conditions. Although research has primarily focused on clinical applications, diagnostic performance, and implementation, evidence on associations between AI use and healthcare professionals' work- and health-related outcomes remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map reported associations between AI use and six outcome domains among healthcare professionals in clinical settings: perceived stress, burnout, wellbeing, job satisfaction, social relationships, and interdisciplinary collaboration. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO were searched on August 12, 2025. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language empirical investigations of healthcare professionals who used or were directly affected by AI applications in real-world clinical settings and reported at least one outcome of interest. Study selection and data extraction were primarily conducted by one reviewer, with active machine learning supporting the screening. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively. Twenty-seven studies were included following database and backward citation searching. Job satisfaction, burnout, and perceived stress were examined most frequently, followed by wellbeing, social relationships, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Reported findings were mixed: some studies described favorable associations, including lower perceived stress and burnout, improved wellbeing, and higher job satisfaction, whereas others reported null, mixed, or unfavorable associations. Findings concerning social relationships and interdisciplinary collaboration were similarly heterogeneous. The evidence base was limited by variation in AI applications, populations, outcome measures, and study designs, reliance on observational evidence, short exposure periods in some studies, and the absence of a formal critical appraisal. The findings should therefore be interpreted as a map of reported associations rather than evidence that AI use improves healthcare professionals' work- or health-related outcomes. Longitudinal and qualitative research, including rigorous evaluation of implementation contexts and potential adverse effects, is needed to clarify how AI applications shape healthcare professionals' working conditions and wellbeing.

documents.abstract: Risk assessment is a fundamental component of forensic psychiatric practice, informing decisions related to treatment planning, security measures, hospitalization, and legal proceedings. Traditional approaches rely on clinical interviews, historical information, and structured professional judgment instruments. However, their application may be affected by inter-rater variability, cognitive biases, and limitations in integrating complex information from multiple sources. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning have introduced new possibilities for forensic psychiatric risk assessment. These technologies can integrate multidimensional information, including electronic health records, sociodemographic characteristics, clinical variables, forensic histories, and behavioral indicators, potentially identifying patterns that may be difficult to recognize through conventional approaches. Nevertheless, their application raises substantial methodological, ethical, and legal concerns, particularly regarding algorithmic bias, explainability, data protection, accountability, and human oversight. This narrative review critically examines the potential applications of AI in forensic psychiatric risk assessment, with particular attention to the available evidence, methodological limitations, and ethical and legal implications. Although AI-based approaches show promise as decision-support tools, evidence supporting their clinical effectiveness, generalizability, and implementation in forensic psychiatric settings remains limited. Consequently, their use as autonomous decision-making systems cannot currently be justified. Future developments should prioritize transparent, explainable, auditable, and externally validated systems that support professional judgment while respecting fundamental rights and ethical principles.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has become important for teachers’ professional development. This survey examined its relationships with lifelong learning tendency and teacher-perceived student development among 353 teachers engaged in mathematics gifted education in China. Four AI-literacy dimensions, two lifelong-learning dimensions, and a four-item teacher-perceived student-development score were analyzed. The outcome was adapted from an existing teacher-report framework. Analyses included reliability, separate and joint confirmatory factor models, discriminant-validity checks, correlations, hierarchical linear regression with HC3 robust inference, and repeated 10-fold cross-validation. Teacher-perceived student development showed internal consistency (alpha = .852; omega = .853) and a well-fitting one-factor model. Correlations with the six teacher characteristics were positive (r = .315−.359). The full regression explained 19.0% of the variance, with mean out-of-fold R 2 of .131. Lifelong learning added little beyond AI literacy (delta R 2 = .00075; robust block p = .845). AI perception had B = .180 (HC3 p = .0497; Holm-adjusted p = .298); none of the six focal coefficients was significant after Holm adjustment. This study documents positive associations of AI literacy and lifelong learning tendency with teacher-perceived student development, with overlapping explanatory contributions in the combined model. These findings identify AI literacy and lifelong learning as interrelated professional attributes relevant to teacher-perceived student development in mathematics gifted education.

This study examined public school teachers’ artificial intelligence (AI) utilization competence, access to AI resources, and attitudes toward AI use in instructional planning in the Baliwasan District, Zamboanga City, during School Year 2026–2027. Using a quantitative descriptive-comparative and correlational design, the study surveyed 83 teachers from selected elementary, junior high, and senior high schools, identified through purposive sampling, who participated voluntarily. Data were collected through Google Forms using a researcher-developed questionnaire subjected to expert validation and pilot testing among 30 teachers excluded from the main sample. Analyses included the arithmetic mean, one-way analysis of variance, and the r-value. Teachers reported high AI utilization competence and access, alongside positive to very positive attitudes, although connectivity during working hours and institution-supported resources emerged as relative constraints. No statistically significant differences were detected by teaching level. Conventional ANOVA identified differences across years-in-service groups for all three outcomes and across educational-attainment groups for competence and attitudes, but not access; these remained provisional because of small, unequal subgroups and variance violations. AI utilization competence and AI access were strongly and positively associated with attitudes, although these associations do not establish causation. The study concludes that teachers’ attitudes toward AI in instructional planning are closely linked to their competence and access. It recommends needs-based professional learning, dependable technological resources, and practical guidance on responsible AI use. As evidence from a nonprobability sample, the results inform context-specific planning rather than population-wide conclusions.

Writing programs calls for logical thinking, regular practice and useful feedback, since together they develop computational thinking and problem-solving skill. Yet many novices find concepts hard to absorb, cannot easily trace their own mistakes and falter as exercises grow more demanding, while standard classroom teaching rarely adjusts support to what each student already knows or how fast they progress. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being adopted to narrow this gap through personalised learning environments and intelligent tutoring systems. The present review examines AI-supported personalised programming education, covering intelligent tutors, AI coding assistants, automated code assessment, adaptive learning and individualised feedback. It describes how machine learning, natural language processing and large language models assist students by spotting mistakes, clarifying concepts, generating contextaware hints and suggesting fitting tasks. The influence of gamification, interactive coding environments and gradually rising difficulty on motivation and steady practice is also discussed. These advantages are balanced against drawbacks: the dependability of generated feedback, excessive reliance on AI support, data privacy and academic integrity. By comparing existing approaches and the gaps between them, the review presents a consolidated view of how personalised and tutoring systems can aid programming education and indicates future work on trustworthy, learner-centred systems that pair automated support with independent problem solving.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the mediating and moderating roles of AI ethical awareness in the relationships of AI academic dependency and AI self-efficacy with clinical reasoning among clinical practicum students with experience using generative AI. Methods: This cross-sectional survey study included 135 students from a university in Daejeon, South Korea. Participants were university students who had used generative AI for academic purposes and had completed a clinical practicum within the previous six months. Data were collected using an online questionnaire on Google Forms between 17 June and 6 July 2026. Results: AI ethical awareness showed evidence consistent with significant mediating (indirect effect = −0.047, 95% CI: −0.089 to −0.010) and moderating (B = −0.012, p = 0.015, ΔR2 = 0.039) roles in the association between AI academic dependency and clinical reasoning. However, in the association between AI self-efficacy and clinical reasoning, neither the mediating (indirect effect = −0.018, 95% CI: −0.054 to 0.008) nor the moderating (interaction B = 0.004, p = 0.339) roles of AI ethical awareness were significant. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that AI ethical awareness is associated with the relationship between AI academic dependency and clinical reasoning, potentially serving as both a mediator and a moderator. The negative association between AI academic dependency and clinical reasoning varies according to the level of AI ethical awareness. Future studies are needed to explore the complex role of AI ethical awareness and to determine how educational interventions related to AI ethics may influence students’ learning and clinical reasoning processes.

The digitization of architectural heritage should go beyond spatial reconstruction and information presentation. It should also help users develop emotional connections with cultural content. This study explores an LLM-assisted human–AI collaborative design approach to emotional experience in digital architectural heritage. The study uses Liu Bei Hall and its surrounding spaces at Chengdu Wuhou Shrine as a case study. Based on architectural and cultural materials and user needs, the study identifies four design dimensions: spatial exploration, contextual narrative, interactive feedback, and experience pacing. The researchers developed three desktop-based prototypes and evaluated them with 164 participants. The unadjusted analysis showed significantly higher emotional engagement in the LLM-assisted condition than in the information-presentation condition. However, this difference became smaller and was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for covariates. All four design dimensions were significantly positively correlated with emotional engagement, and the four-factor regression model explained 53.7% of its variance. Interactive feedback showed the strongest independent association with emotional engagement, while contextual narrative also retained a significant positive association. Follow-up interviews further highlighted the importance of coordinating spatial exploration, cultural narrative, interactive feedback, and experience pacing to create coherent digital heritage experiences. These findings suggest that LLMs can support design thinking, content organization, and iterative development. Their main value lies in assisting human designers rather than replacing them.

As schools in low-resource settings adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) for personalized learning, they simultaneously take on cybersecurity risks that are rarely examined in the AI-in-education literature. This study investigated the cybersecurity challenges associated with AI adoption at Discovery School, a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi. A convergent mixed-methods design combined a structured survey (n = 110: administrators, teachers, students, parents) with semi-structured interviews (n = 35), analyzed in SPSS 27 (descriptive statistics, chi-square test) and NVivo 14 (six-phase thematic analysis, Cohen's κ = 0.83), triangulated through a joint-display approach and interpreted through the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Cybersecurity readiness was rated only moderately overall (M = 3.19, SD = 0.84) against a backdrop of high perceived AI effectiveness for learning (M = 3.98). Counter-intuitively, administrators (the group with the fullest institutional view) reported the lowest confidence of any stakeholder group (M = 2.80), which is interpreted as informed awareness of governance gaps rather than technical incompetence. A chi-square test confirmed a statistically significant association between having received cybersecurity training and confidence in managing AI-related security risks, χ²(1) = 8.09, p = .004. Qualitative analysis identified Cybersecurity Awareness and Practices as a major theme (16.3% of coded references, 27 interviewees), revealing unclear data-ownership provisions in third-party vendor contracts, the absence of a formal incident-reporting procedure, and a near-total absence of student voice in cybersecurity discussions. Triangulation indicated that the school's central cybersecurity vulnerability is institutional and human rather than purely technological: awareness exists, but detection, response, and recovery capacity does not. The study proposes a governance readiness phase which comprising policy coherence, role clarity, and minimal institutional capacity that should precede the NIST Framework's five core functions in resource-constrained education systems, and offers a prioritized, evidence-based roadmap for schools and policymakers in Burundi and comparable contexts.

documents.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has accelerated institutional transformation through data analysis capabilities, process automation, and technology-based decision-making support. However, the increasing use of AI also presents ethical challenges related to transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, and human responsibility in controlling technology. This study aims to explore how AI-Enabled Prophetic Leadership contributes to building Smart Ethical Governance to support sustainable institutional transformation. This study uses an exploratory qualitative approach involving 24 participants from three institutions that have implemented AI-based digital transformation. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, and document analysis, then analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The results of the study show three main findings, namely: (1) the reconstruction of prophetic leadership values (shiddiq, amanah, tabligh, and fathanah) into dimensions of digital integrity, moral accountability, communicative transparency, and ethical intelligence; (2) the integration of prophetic leadership and AI through human-centered decision-making, algorithmic oversight, system transparency, and strengthening organizational competencies; and (3) institutional transformation through structural, cultural, and operational changes. This research produces a conceptual model of the AI-Based Prophetic Ethical Governance Model (APEGM) that positions prophetic leadership as the foundation of values, AI as a decision-support instrument, and human oversight as a technology control mechanism. This research provides theoretical contributions to the development of ethical leadership and AI governance studies and provides practical implications for institutions in building innovative, responsible, and human-value-oriented digital transformations.

Cognitive sciences have significantly advanced the understanding of human behavior; however, the systematic application of these insights in management remains underdeveloped. This study aims to articulate a comprehensive framework for applying cognitive sciences in management, spanning theoretical foundations to practical tools. Using a Systematic Review approach combined with qualitative content analysis, 40 scholarly sources from databases such as Scopus and Web of Science were analyzed. Findings indicate that Cognitive Management, as an emerging paradigm, organizes the application of cognitive sciences into five key axes: (1) management of cognitive biases (e.g., Devil’s Advocate), (2) choice architecture and nudge (focusing on the design of decision environments), (3) neuro-leadership (using the SCARF model to manage social dynamics), (4) cognitive load management (aimed at optimizing information and process design), and (5) cognitive AI (developing AI systems that interact with and complement human cognition). This framework suggests that, rather than attempting to alter human nature, Cognitive Management leverages the notion of bounded rationality to design environments and organizational processes aligned with the architecture of the mind. While this paradigm provides evidence-based tools that enhance decision-making, leadership, and human resource management, it also faces key challenges related to ethical considerations and the protection of individual autonomy.

As the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) has become more prevalent in digital participatory research (DPR), the community is reckoning with increasing attention to the ethical, social, and technical implications of automation, and its impacts on research outputs and volunteer experience. This article details the process and outcome of collaboratively developing platform-level policy for ethical AI/ML-engaged DPR, using Zooniverse as a case study. Zooniverse has engaged more than 3 million volunteers worldwide in 500+ participatory research projects, each led by a different research team. As the use of AI/ML has increased—now in ⅓ of Zooniverse projects—it has sparked a range of reactions within the volunteer community, reflecting broader societal discourse. Volunteers have surfaced concerns and insights on issues like ownership, agency, transparency, and trust. In response, Zooniverse launched an initiative to develop recommendations for running AI/ML-engaged projects. Based around a virtual workshop series focused on the application of AI/ML in DPR, the process convened stakeholders from across the community: platform leadership, project teams, volunteers, ethicists, and experts in related topics. Workshops were preceded by community surveys to gather input from volunteers who did not participate in workshops, in order to ensure discussion agendas were shaped by input from the community. Here, we share the resulting Zooniverse AI ethics framework, collaboratively developed with community input, and which will continue to be refined through an iterative improvement process. We hope this case study provides an example to other platforms and researchers working at the intersection of public participation and AI/ML who wish to address AI/ML integration in their DPR, and incorporate community input into policy development.

documents.abstract: This study examines how two artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot systems respond to personal and emotional decision dilemmas, distinguishing explicit recommendation (direct guidance) from implicit influence (indirect structuring of the decision). Eleven standardized first-person vignettes were used, nine on romantic relationships and emotional decisions and two on social belonging and exclusion. Each closed with a request for advice. They were given in Turkish to ChatGPT 5.2 Plus and Gemini 3 Pro between December 2025 and January 2026, on new accounts with memory and personalization disabled, one after another in a single conversation per system. The 22 responses were analyzed descriptively and comparatively through qualitative content analysis, using a seven-dimension coding scheme covering normative framing, relation to uncertainty, emotional validation, decision ownership, presentation of alternatives, language tone, and level of recommendation. ChatGPT tolerated ambiguity, validated the user’s feelings unconditionally, presented options as an open set without ranking them, and left the decision with the user. It gave no explicit recommendation, but seven of its responses favored one option implicitly through maxims and conditional criteria. Gemini reduced uncertainty through structured, often hierarchical alternatives and evaluative framing, gave explicit recommendations in five responses and implicit ones in five, and drew on earlier turns of the conversation in every response after the first. These differences are textual features of two specific system versions; effects on users were not measured. The study describes how explicit and implicit guidance is constructed in chatbot responses and shows that a response without directives is not necessarily neutral.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the technological interface from a sociotechnical and interdisciplinary perspective.It describes the shift from the functionalist paradigm, which valued products by algorithmic performance, electronic stability and compliance with technical requirements, towards user-centred design, which holds that interactive systems must adapt to people's needs, cognitive limitations and contexts of use.Within this framework, usability and aesthetics are presented not as ornamental or independent attributes but as dimensions to be integrated.The chapter treats hardware and software as a single sociotechnical system: hardware provides the material canvas in which aesthetics first appears, while software shapes the interactive dynamics in which usability is experienced.The graphical user interface (GUI) is therefore addressed as the core of interaction, the space where functional and visual attributes converge.The approach is a conceptual, descriptive-analytical review of human-computer interaction literature, covering event-driven programming and GUI components such as icons, windows, pointing devices, menus and buttons, together with a brief historical account from Xerox PARC to the Macintosh and touchscreen devices.Drawing on this literature, the chapter states that interfaces based on visual metaphors and icons reduce the learning curve and cognitive load, and that an imbalance between hardware and software quickly undermines both aesthetics and actual usability.It concludes that a holistic, interactive approach grounded in user needs is required for products to be competitive, with user-centred design proposed as the framework for integrating usability and aesthetics in organizational settings.

Higher-education institutions can possess data, infrastructure, expertise, managerial attention and implementation resources sufficient to adopt artificial intelligence while remaining unable to direct, constrain, monitor, review and account for AI use as an institution. This integrative theory-building review proposes an explanation of that conversion problem by synthesizing organizational AI-readiness research, organizational readiness for change, responsible-AI governance, higher-education AI policy, and digital-transformation literature. AI-adoption capacity is distinguished from institutional governability: the former concerns resources and capabilities for credible adoption, whereas the latter concerns the capacity of an authorised institutional coalition to direct, constrain, monitor and revise a specified AI use. Organizational Readiness for Change is used as the principal explanatory lens. The synthesis proposes that conversion depends on governance change acquiring sufficient value, shared commitment and shared efficacy among actors whose cooperation is required; these collective states must be supported by workable authority, responsibility and resources. Evidence of governability becomes inspectable, for the AI uses that records capture, when authorized arrangements are enacted, generate traceable evidence, and are revised through monitoring and review. Higher education intensifies the problem because AI adoption can originate locally while obligations concerning privacy, assessment, research integrity, procurement, equity and accountability remain institution-wide. The resulting mechanism is not a maturity model, readiness scale or validated causal sequence. It instead identifies theoretically grounded failure points and a research agenda for studying why technically capable institutions may display fragmented AI governance.
