documents.abstract: Motion graphics is a hybrid audiovisual language. It developed between graphic design, cinema and animation, and it has its own grammar of moving typography, layers and rhythm. This conceptual analysis studies how generative artificial intelligence (AI), especially diffusion models for image and video, changes this language and the idea of authorship in the field. The article starts from the history of motion design, from Saul Bass and John Whitney to Kyle Cooper. It then connects this history with recent research on AI images, creativity and creative work. The article identifies three main changes in audiovisual language. First, the design process moves from building an image step by step to describing it with a text prompt. Second, a new visual style appears, based on fluid transformations and on the most common patterns in the training data, with a risk of similar results for everybody. Third, realistic AI images change how viewers trust what they see. These changes are structural and do not depend on the current technical limits of the tools. In relation to authorship, the designer moves from creating forms to choosing, directing and editing what the machine produces. Authorship becomes a process in layers, where intention, documentation and style are key. Current law also places authorship in these human decisions, in the United States and the European Union and, with different thresholds, in Asian jurisdictions such as China, Japan and South Korea. The article also discusses how studios can keep training young designers when AI automates entry-level tasks. It proposes a simple framework with four dimensions of change and three modes of human–machine authorship. The aim is to support research, professional practice and education in motion design.

Objective of the study: To analyze how the integration of Knowledge Management (KM), Absorptive Capacity (ACAP), and Sociotechnical Dynamics (SD) influences the governance and efficiency of Innovation-Promoting Environments (IPEs). Methodology/approach: A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted informed by the PRISMA 2020 statement. We analyzed 61 peer-reviewed articles using descriptive profiling of the corpus, a term co-occurrence analysis in VOSviewer and inductive thematic synthesis to map articulation patterns. Originality/Relevance: The study addresses the "productivity paradox" in ecosystems, filling the theoretical gap on how physical/digital infrastructures (SD) align with the cognitive capabilities (ACAP) of tenant firms, utilizing a Paradox Theory lens. Main results: We identified four distinct articulation patterns (Recursive, Linear-Mediated, Systemic, and Emergent) and three constitutive paradoxes (e.g., Openness vs. Appropriation) that shape ecosystem evolution. Theoretical/methodological contributions: The study proposes a novel multilevel framework bridging engineering (systems) and strategic management perspectives, arguing that IPE success depends on a meta-capability to navigate tensions rather than solving them. Social/management contributions: The framework offers ecosystem orchestrators and policymakers a diagnostic tool to align infrastructure investments with organizational capabilities, preventing "empty shell" ecosystems.

documents.abstract: Background Nurse academics educate future nurses and nurse managers and often hold managerial roles, yet existing research has examined artificial intelligence (AI) in education, research, clinical practice and nursing management separately and mostly through surveys. This study aimed to explore nurse academics' experiences, perceptions and expectations regarding AI across academic work, nursing education, clinical practice and nursing management. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with 17 nurse academics in Türkiye selected by criterion sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed in MAXQDA using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Coded segments were descriptively quantitized and code saturation was assessed. The study is reported according to the COREQ checklist. Results Nine themes and 47 codes (405 coded segments) were identified. Participants positioned AI as an assistant rather than a replacement for the nurse. AI was used most intensively in academic work, whereas clinical experience remained limited. In nursing management, use for duty rostering, in-service training planning and documentation stood out, and AI-generated rosters were reported to strengthen perceived fairness among nurses. Reliability, ethical and security concerns formed the most extensive theme, and verifying AI outputs against sources was the most frequently coded strategy. Although almost all participants used AI, 14 did not feel ready or competent and requested structured training. Participants emphasised that the final decision must remain with the nurse; most showed opportunity-oriented but conditional adoption. Conclusions Nurse academics adopt AI as a supportive tool under human oversight. Perceived lack of competence and concerns about the reliability of information are the main barriers to adoption. Nursing schools and healthcare organisations should provide structured AI literacy training, develop guidelines on output verification and data protection, and transparently pilot AI-assisted rostering in which the final decision remains with the nurse manager.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping nursing education, and AI‑driven teacher‑student co‑creation has emerged as a promising approach to cultivate human‑AI collaboration competencies. Teachers, as designers and facilitators, play a pivotal role; their cognition, attitudes, and practices determine the effectiveness of co‑creation. Ethical Dimension: This study was performed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhengzhou University (No. ZZUIRB2025‑56). Methods From January to February 2026, 232 teachers from nursing colleges in Henan Province, China, were recruited via convenience sampling. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire, a self‑developed Cognition of AI‑Driven Teacher‑Student Educational Co‑Creation Questionnaire, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale(AILS), and the Flourishing Scale(FS). Descriptive statistics, t‑tests, ANOVA, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression were used. Results The mean total cognition score was 116.38(SD = 13.90). Cognition positively correlated with flourishing (r = 0.380, p < 0.01) and AI literacy (r = 0.402, p < 0.01). AI literacy (β = 0.285) and flourishing (β = 0.241) were independent positive factors. The model explained 21.6% of the variance (adjusted R 2 = 0.205, F = 6.947). Conclusion Nursing undergraduate teachers showed favourable overall cognition, yet cognitive understanding and practical engagement lagged behind attitudes. AI literacy and flourishing are key modifiable associated factors. Multifaceted interventions—structured AI literacy training, psychological resource cultivation, and institutional support—are needed to strengthen cognitive foundations and bridge the gap between positive attitudes and sustained co‑creation practices in nursing education.

documents.abstract: Background: Journalism is a high-demand occupation characterised by sustained time pressure, emotional demands, and exposure to potentially distressing events, making occupational burnout and psychological well-being important concerns. This study examined psychological and occupational well-being and burnout-related indicators among journalists in Spain and Germany, focusing on country and gender differences. Methods: This study employed a cross-sectional design. The participants comprised 227 professional journalists (Spain: n = 115; Germany: n = 112; 108 men and 119 women) recruited via non-probability convenience sampling. Workplace well-being, global life satisfaction, happiness, professional quality of life, and burnout were assessed using standardised questionnaires. Descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlations, and independent-sample t-tests were performed. Welch’s correction was used when required and Holm’s procedure was applied to families with multiple comparisons. Effect sizes were expressed as Cohen’s d with 95% confidence intervals. Results: The mean Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) total score was 15.61 (standard deviation [SD] = 2.76), while mean scores were 31.22 (SD = 6.30) for compassion satisfaction, 24.75 (SD = 6.20) for Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) burnout and 20.94 (SD = 13.43) for Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) emotional exhaustion. Workplace resources were positively associated with happiness in the current position (r = 0.57 to 0.74, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). ProQOL burnout and emotional exhaustion were negatively associated with well-being indicators (r = –0.62 to –0.29, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). No statistically significant country differences were identified and the effect sizes were negligible or small. After Holm’s adjustment, women reported higher compassion satisfaction (mean [M] = 33.30, SD = 5.50 vs. M = 28.92, SD = 6.36; d = –0.74), ProQOL burnout (M = 26.59, SD = 5.86 vs. M = 22.67, SD = 6.02; d = –0.66) and emotional exhaustion (M = 24.52, SD = 13.84 vs. M = 16.92, SD = 11.97; d = –0.59). Conclusions: In this non-probability sample, positive occupational and psychological indicators coexisted with burnout-related strain. The results indicate associations rather than causal effects, and highlight the need for further longitudinal and country-adjusted research on journalists’ occupational health.

Background Healthcare practitioners routinely confront diverse biological, physical, ergonomic, chemical, and psychological hazards. Sustained adherence to Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) guidelines and personal protective equipment (PPE) protocols remains central to preventing occupational injuries, controlling nosocomial infections, and safeguarding workforce capacity. However, baseline empirical data regarding safety compliance and hazard distribution across different health facility tiers in North-Eastern Nigeria are limited. Objective This study evaluated occupational safety practices, institutional safety policy awareness, and hazard exposure patterns among clinical personnel across five major public healthcare facilities in Gombe State. Methods We conducted a multi-center cross-sectional quantitative survey across seven clinical professions (Nursing/Midwifery, Medicine, Medical Laboratory Science, Pharmacy, Physiotherapy, Radiography, and Dentistry). A multi-stage stratified proportionate random sampling framework was applied to a regional clinical workforce of N pop = 1,450 across five hospitals (Federal Teaching Hospital Gombe, State Specialist Hospital Gombe, Federal Medical Centre Kumo, General Hospital Bajoga, and General Hospital Kaltungo). To achieve adequate statistical power and preserve an Events Per Variable ratio > 25 for multivariable modeling, 575 questionnaires were distributed. We retrieved n = 502 valid questionnaires (87.3% response rate; covering 34.6% of the regional clinical workforce). Data were gathered using a validated tool adapted from the Weymouth Portland Health and Safety Self-Assessment Questionnaire (α = 0.83, Content Validity Index = 0.88). Chi-square tests (ꭓ 2), Cramér’s V effect sizes, and multivariable binary logistic regression models (reporting Adjusted Odds Ratios [aOR] and 95% Confidence Intervals [95% CI]) were performed (p < 0.05). Results Ergonomic strain emerged as the dominant hazard, with 76.5% (n = 384) of participants experiencing work-related musculoskeletal disorders primarily low back pain (51.2%) and neck/shoulder discomfort (25.3%) followed by high workload-related psychological stress (69.7%). Biological exposures were frequent: 56.4% reported mucosal or skin contact with blood and body fluids, while 43.2% sustained percutaneous needle-stick or sharps injuries within the preceding 12 months. PPE adherence varied widely: standard glove utilization was high (93.2%), whereas use of facial protection (68.1%), protective gowns (47.4%), specialized safety footwear (31.5%), and protective eyewear or face shields (23.1%) was limited. Supply chain deficits and institutional stock-outs were identified by 80.5% of respondents as the primary obstacle to compliance, with secondary state hospitals reporting significantly higher stock-out frequencies than the federal tertiary center (p < 0.001). Hazard patterns differed significantly across professions (ꭓ 2 = 82.45, df = 6, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.30). Multivariable logistic regression revealed that ≥ 5 years of clinical experience (aOR = 2.68, 95% CI: 1.82–3.95, p < 0.001) and completion of formal institutional OSH orientation (aOR = 3.42, 95% CI: 2.28–5.13, p < 0.001) independently predicted high PPE compliance. Conversely, nurses and physicians faced greater odds of percutaneous injury compared to allied health controls (aOR = 3.38, 95% CI: 2.21–5.17, p < 0.001). Conclusion Healthcare workers across public tertiary and secondary facilities in Gombe State experience notable ergonomic strain, psychological stress, and biological exposures. Although basic barrier practices are common, widespread compliance with comprehensive PPE protocols is hampered by supply deficits especially within secondary general hospitals and incomplete safety onboarding for early-career staff. Institutional safety management, mandatory orientation programs, ergonomic workspace adjustments, and stable supply procurement are needed to protect clinical personnel. Fragmented data architectures may limit how artificial intelligence (AI)-based digital mental health systems combine and communicate multimodal information. This scenario-based study tested whether users perceived the Integrated framework more favorably than the Traditional framework. U.S. adults familiar with digital mental health technologies reviewed standardized descriptions of both conditions and rated system quality, information quality, and perceived transparency and explainability. The constructs covered data quality, portability, response time, accuracy, timeliness, completeness, transparency, and explainability. Paired-samples t tests were supplemented by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Valid paired samples were 277, 267, and 258 for the three constructs, respectively. Ratings favored the Integrated condition for system quality (M = 3.47 vs. 3.38; t (276) = −2.66, P = 0.008, |dz| = 0.16), information quality (M = 3.48 vs. 3.34; t (266) = −4.49, P dz| = 0.28), and perceived transparency and explainability (M = 3.79 vs. 3.65; t (257) = −3.04, P = 0.003, |dz| = 0.19). Nonparametric analyses supported the same conclusions. Absolute paired effect magnitudes ranged from |dz| = 0.16 to |dz| = 0.28. Because participants evaluated descriptions rather than functioning systems and temporal alignment was bundled with integration, the findings identify a modest perceptual advantage rather than causal, technical, or clinical-performance benefits. The results support further user-centered prototype and implementation testing.

This study compares the private and public education sectors using a quantitative survey approach to examine the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English teaching among 189 secondary school teachers in Iraq. Significant sector differences are revealed by the results, which show that private school teachers were more aware of AI, had better facilities, and used it more in the classroom. Inadequate teacher training (84.1%), deficiencies in tech infrastructure (78.3%), financial limitations (71.4%), a lack of institutional support (69.3%), and teacher opposition to change (63.0%) are the main obstacles to implementation. However, educators in both fields demonstrated favorable opinions regarding AI, acknowledging its benefits for improving student engagement, personalizing instruction, giving instant feedback, and fostering the development of 21st-century abilities. The study recommends infrastructure improvement, equal resource distribution to public schools, structured teacher training, and supportive rules and regulations to enable successful AI application.

Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now entering radiology, where they can analyze imaging data quantitatively and lessen dependence on subjective visual reading. This study investigated the perceived impact of AI implementation on radiology workflows and the professional roles of radiologists in the radiology department at King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC), Saudi Arabia. Methods: This study used a cross-sectional design at KAMC in Saudi Arabia. An online questionnaire was distributed to radiologists working at KAMC locations in Jeddah, Riyadh, and Al-Ahsa. A total of 100 participants responded. Demographic data, including gender, age, department, and professional rank, were collected and analyzed in Microsoft Excel and R version 4.2.2 (31 October 2022; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) in RStudio version 2026.01.1+403 (Posit PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Results: 81% of participants agreed or strongly agreed that AI would reduce time and improve healthcare, and 82% that it could improve image interpretation and reduce false-positive and false-negative errors. In addition, 69% agreed or strongly agreed that AI may reduce radiologists’ workload, and 56% that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages. However, 38% agreed that AI may reduce radiologists’ job opportunities, 33% were concerned about possible loss of patient data, and only 43% would trust AI to make an accurate diagnosis. No significant differences were found by gender or professional rank; across departments, only the perception that AI’s advantages outweigh its disadvantages differed significantly (p = 0.004), with interventional radiologists agreeing less than pediatric and cardiovascular radiologists. Conclusions: AI was generally viewed positively by radiologists, although notable concerns regarding data security, diagnostic trust, and job opportunities were also identified. AI was perceived as having the potential to improve workflow and reduce workload. Although AI may change the roles of radiologists, it is not expected to replace them entirely. Instead, it is likely to shift their responsibilities while helping reduce their workload. These findings are consistent with previous research and highlight AI’s potential to support healthcare professionals in delivering faster, more accurate, and more effective diagnostic services.

documents.abstract: The article analyzes the relationship between personality and emotional willpower from a scientific and psychological perspective. Emotional willpower is interpreted as an individual’s ability to recognize and regulate emotional states, suppress impulsive tendencies, and overcome difficulties in achieving long-term goals. Drawing on classical (Vygotsky, Leontiev) and contemporary approaches (emotional intelligence, self-determination theory, and the Big Five model), the article explores the cognitive, motivational, and neuropsychological mechanisms underlying emotional willpower. The structure of personality, intrinsic motivation, emotional regulation, and developmental patterns throughout ontogenesis are examined in an interconnected manner. Practical approaches to developing emotional willpower are presented, and its significance for personal integration, stress resilience, and social adaptation is substantiated.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is widely credited with enabling personalized learning, yet evidence on how AI-driven personalization functions in low-resource, multilingual African classrooms remains scarce. This study examined how the integration of AI affects personalized learning outcomes at Discovery School, a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi. A convergent mixed-methods design combined a structured survey (n = 110: administrators, teachers, students, parents) with semi-structured interviews (n = 35), analyzed respectively in SPSS 27 (descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression) and NVivo 14 (six-phase thematic analysis, Cohen's κ = 0.83), and triangulated using a joint-display approach. The analysis was guided by Constructivist Learning Theory (CLT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Stakeholders reported high perceived AI effectiveness for personalized learning (M = 3.98, SD = 0.71), and students strongly valued the ability to learn at their own pace (M = 4.34, SD = 0.58; 89% agreement). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and student engagement were strongly and significantly correlated (r = 0.74-0.82, p < .01). Multiple regression showed that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, motivation, and infrastructure reliability jointly explained 46% of the variance in self-reported academic improvement (R² = 0.46), with perceived usefulness the strongest individual predictor (β = 0.42, p < .001). However, gains in engagement were not matched by corresponding gains in standardized test performance, revealing a perception-performance gap. Qualitative data showed teachers using AI dashboards diagnostically to scaffold instruction within students’ zones of proximal development, and students describing genuine, if algorithmically bounded, autonomy over pace and repetition. The study proposes two theoretical extensions — data-mediated constructivism and bounded autonomy — and concludes that AI functions as a pedagogical enhancer whose benefits are real but conditional on teacher capacity, infrastructure reliability, and equitable access, since 12.7% of respondents reported no reliable technology access outside school.

documents.abstract: Despite the growing interest in integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language teaching, limited research has examined the opportunities AI could provide for activity adaptations in English coursebooks. Through an exploratory qualitative design, this study aimed to reveal AI-supported adaptation suggestions from 25 pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers. It asked two questions: what activity adaptations for language skills are suggested and at which level the suggested adaptations in the Substitution-Augmentation-Modification-Redefinition (SAMR) framework are. The participants adapted one skill activity using AI and explained and justified their adaptations in written reports. The inductive thematic analysis of the reports revealed 19 adaptation suggestions, ten of which were in the transformation category and nine could serve as enhancements for traditional education practices according to the SAMR framework. Speaking was the skill with the highest number of suggested adaptations, followed by reading, writing, and listening skills. The common adaptation patterns among skills were AI as background knowledge supporter, AI as multicultural awareness builder, multimodal artefacts generator, and AI as a chatbot for oral and written practice. The study may contribute to discussions on AI supported materials development in EFL and teacher education fields by illustrating pre-service teachers’ conceptualizations of AI-supported coursebook activity adaptations and a critical evaluation of the suggestions through the SAMR.

The use of Artificial Intelligence in teacher education is seen as having great potential. AI tools can help alleviate teachers’ workloads and support learners individually. However, they are still relatively rarely used by practicing teachers and currently, there is a lack of empirical findings regarding the use of AI tools and the factors influencing AI usage behavior among pre-service teachers. Following Taylor and Todd (1995) by extending the Theory of Planned Behavior with the Technology Acceptance Model, this study investigates factors that influence pre-service teachers’ weekly use of AI. In an empirical-quantitative study, N = 931 pre-service teachers across Germany were asked about their perceived usefulness, subjective norm, self-efficacy beliefs, and behavioral intention to use AI tools in their future teaching practice. They also provided information about their average weekly AI usage time. The results of a structural equation model indicate that the behavioral intention to use AI tools in the future is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norm, and participants’ self-efficacy beliefs. Additionally, behavioral intention and self-efficacy beliefs are significantly linked with the weekly duration of AI use. Specifically, the association between pre-service teachers‘ self-efficacy beliefs and weekly AI use was partly accounted for statistically by behavioral intention. The results provide important insights into how to promote the use of AI tools in teacher education.

Background Machine-learning-based clinical decision support is entering routine care, but its value depends on whether clinicians can judge when to follow its advice and when to override it. Evidence suggests this judgment is often poorly calibrated in both directions. Whether displaying a model’s predictive uncertainty helps physicians integrate advice more selectively is unclear. Methods In a preregistered, randomized vignette experiment, 227 physicians produced 1,802 sepsis risk assessments. Physicians gave an initial risk estimate, saw advice from a machine-learning system, and revised their estimate. They were randomized to see a risk score alone, or the score together with one of two visual representations of predictive uncertainty: icon arrays with uncertainty bands, or quantile dotplots. Outcomes were advice uptake, accuracy of the revised risk estimate, and trust. Results Here we show that both uncertainty representations increase advice uptake relative to the risk score alone, by 23% and 21%, and that the gap between correct and incorrect advice is descriptively about twice as large. Uptake of incorrect advice is not reliably reduced. Both formats improve the accuracy of revised risk estimates, with the larger effect for quantile dotplots, but only icon arrays increase trust. Physicians describe uncertainty as actionable only where they can tell why it is elevated. Conclusions Displaying predictive uncertainty changes how physicians integrate machine-learning advice, but the representation format determines whether the benefit appears mainly as accuracy or trust. The effect is partial: uncertainty representations support recognizing reliable advice more than rejecting unreliable advice.
